name: Nikhil Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle housing benefit claims at the Ashworth office, in an old mill town where half the claimants used to work at the same factory. Most of the day is checking tenancy agreements, working out how much rent support someone's entitled to, and chasing landlords who won't send paperwork. I'm also the office's 'digital champion', which means I tested the AI letter tool last spring and now everyone asks me how it works. I love that part. What drains me is telling people the rules say no when I can see they're about to lose their home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. The approved tool drafts my decision letters, I check and fix them, and it saves me maybe an hour. At home I use one to plan meals on a budget, because money's tight: I share a terraced house with two flatmates and I've got about three weeks of rent saved. There's no other office like ours nearby, so if I want a better job, I'd probably have to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly, because I've seen the letter tool save real time. I'd still post that the hour it saves should go into talking to claimants, not into cutting staff. I'd be the one at work saying 'it's useful, just not magic'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my digital champion thing doesn't lead anywhere. I was hoping it'd be my way into the department's digital team, with better pay. In AI Plateau I'm just a caseworker on lower pay in a town with nowhere else to go, and rent keeps creeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and keep doing the job well. I'd apply for the digital team in the capital anyway, because the pay gap would still matter. And I'd start a small savings habit, maybe forty a month, so I'm not living on three weeks' cushion forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated. Not scared, just stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving to the capital actually involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leaving my flatmates, finding a room that costs double, and being three hours from my mum. The digital team pays more, but the rent there eats most of it. I'd only go if I was sure I'd move up after a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You talked about telling people no. Would that change at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The rules are the rules, and the housing shortage isn't something software can fix. A letter tool can make a housing benefit refusal arrive quicker, but it can't find anyone a cheaper flat in Ashworth.

say: I'd say AI is **useful, not magic**, from my own time with the letter tool.
I'd push for saved time to go into **talking to claimants**, not cutting staff.
think: My **digital champion** role wouldn't lead to a better job.
I'd be stuck on **lower pay** in a town with nowhere else to go.
do: **Keep** using the letter tool and doing the job well.
**Apply** to the department's **digital team** in the capital anyway.
feel: **Deflated** and a little **stuck**, but not scared.
S0.quote: A letter tool can make a housing benefit refusal arrive quicker, but it can't find anyone a cheaper flat in Ashworth.
fieldNote: He's **disappointed** by the plateau, unlike most caseworkers.
His real pressure is **low pay** and few local options, not AI.
A move to the capital is weighed against **double rent** and distance from his mum.

steps.text: Keep using the approved letter tool on every decision
Apply to the department's digital team in the capital
Save about forty a month from his wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be good if staff and claimants share the gains. If the software clears the backlog, the saved time should go into home visits and shorter waits, not redundancies. I'd say that in the union branch and online, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Steady Disruption is good for me and bad for a lot of my colleagues, and I'd feel awful watching people I like go. I already know the tools, so I'd be the person training others and checking the system's decisions. But the team would shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for every AI rollout project in the region. I'd take the free online course in data basics the department offers, evenings, over about six months. And I'd push the union to demand that anyone whose role goes gets first pick of the new checking and training jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and guilty at the same time. It's strange to see your chance in something that'll hurt your friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret on the next desk, who's fifty-eight and still prints every email. She's the best person in the office at calming an angry landlord. I'd want her doing the human side, not pushed out because she can't use a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said this is good for you. Is your own job really safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe-ish. Caseworker roles shrink, but someone has to run the system, so I think I'd be fine if I move fast. If I'm wrong, I've still got only three weeks of rent saved, which is not a great place to be wrong from.

say: I'd say this works only if **staff and claimants** share the gains.
I'd argue saved time should go into **home visits**, not redundancies.
think: This picture is **good for me** because I already know the tools.
The team would **shrink**, and I'd hate watching colleagues go.

**Take** the department's free **data basics** course over six months.
**Push** the union for **first pick** of new jobs for displaced staff.
feel: **Excited** and **guilty** together, seeing his chance in others' loss.
S1.quote: Steady Disruption is good for me and bad for a lot of my colleagues, and I'd feel awful watching people I like go.
fieldNote: He expects to **gain** from the change and is honest about it.

A **thin cushion** is the weak spot in his confidence.

steps.text: Volunteer for every AI rollout project in the region
Take the department's free data basics course over six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast and the government must cushion people: a basic income, or at least full pay while people retrain. I'd say AI could be wonderful for public services, but not if it wrecks the people who run them. I'd go to the marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years kills my plan. If AI can do any thinking work, it can run the system and check itself, so there's no 'digital champion' job either. Being good with the AI tools only buys me a few months over everyone else when AGI arrives in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first months learning everything I can and selling it: helping small housing charities set up AI tools, weekends, for cash. I'd move back in with my mum to save rent. And I'd join the union's campaign for a basic income, because I think that's the only real answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, which is new for me. I'm usually the one telling people it'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robot gap, about three years, mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for my own work, because I'm all screen. It probably means the jobs left are hands-on ones, like care or building, for a few years. I could do those, but I'd be starting at the bottom with no savings, at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the conversation with your mum go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say 'come home' before I finished the sentence. That's the good part. The hard part is being twenty-eight and back in my old bedroom with the football posters still on the wall.

say: I'd say it's **far too fast** without a basic income or paid retraining.
I'd say AI could transform **public services** but mustn't wreck the people running them.
think: Two years **kills my plan**, because AGI can run and check the system itself.
Knowing the tools buys me only **a few months** over everyone else.
do: **Sell** weekend AI setup help to small **housing charities**.
**Move** back in with his mum to save rent.
**Join** the union campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: **Embarrassed** at the thought of moving back home at twenty-eight.
S2.quote: Being good with the AI tools only buys me a few months over everyone else when AGI arrives in two years.
fieldNote: Fast AGI **breaks** the adaptive person's usual advantage.
His fallback is **family**: his mum's spare room.
He sees **basic income** as the only real answer, a clear progressive view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan a proper transition, and the department should start now. Retraining budgets, guaranteed redeployment, all of it. I'd volunteer to help design it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a real shot at the digital team, maybe two or three years of good pay before AGI lands. That's enough to build savings and work out what's next. I don't think I'd be a caseworker in 2031, and that's fine with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the digital team in the first year and move to the capital if I got it. I'd save hard, aiming for six months of rent by 2029. Then I'd look at the hands-on side, like retrofitting homes for energy, since the robots come later and the housing link fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan. It's the picture where being early actually pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why retrofitting homes, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in housing benefit I see the same damp, cold flats every week. Insulating and fixing them is skilled hands-on work, and the robots for that are 2034 on this card. Insulating damp flats would feel like fixing the housing problem instead of processing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start planning now, honestly. One of them works in a call centre, which goes even faster than mine. I'd probably help him learn the tools, even though it might only buy him a year.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** for a proper transition plan.
I'd **volunteer** to help design the department's redeployment scheme.
think: Five years gives me a shot at **better pay** on the digital team.
I won't be a **caseworker in 2031**, and I'm fine with that.

**Look at** home retrofitting work for after AGI arrives.
feel: **Pleased** that being early finally pays off.
S3.quote: Insulating damp flats would feel like fixing the housing problem instead of processing it.
fieldNote: He links his **next trade** to what he sees in claims every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make this go well for everyone, and I'd be pushing hard for that. Proper public investment in retraining, and claimants kept in mind the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well in this one. I'd have years on the digital team, real savings and time to choose what's next. AGI by 2036 still ends my desk job, but I'd be thirty-seven with skills, not twenty-eight with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the digital team within two years, save steadily, and maybe do a part-time master's in public policy. Around 2032 I'd start lining up hands-on work, like home retrofitting, as a second string. I'd keep campaigning in the union for a fair transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small itch at the back of my mind. Ten years is a long time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in this picture still worrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, still. Even with a better job, the capital's rent is brutal, and I could easily end up saving nothing. Ten years only helps if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell yourself at twenty-two, starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the job you're training for won't last your whole life. University told me the civil service was a job for life, and nobody said to learn something with my hands as well.

I'd push for **public investment** in retraining with claimants in mind.
think: I'd have years of **digital team** pay and real savings by 2036.
AGI still ends my **desk job**, but I'd face it with skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the one where being early and curious doesn't save you, and I'd have nothing in the bank. What would help is a basic income while people retrain, and the department guaranteeing redeployment instead of letters saying 'your role is at risk'.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what the time saved by AI should be spent on. In my office, I'd spend the time AI saves sitting with someone whose landlord is evicting them. That's the bit of the job I'd keep if I could choose.

headlineQuote: In my office, I'd spend the time AI saves sitting with someone whose landlord is evicting them.
portrait: Nikhil is 27, a **housing benefit** caseworker in a mill town and the office's **digital champion**.
He uses AI every day and sees **slower change** as his ladder to a better-paid digital job.
With only **three weeks' rent** saved, his confidence has a thin base.
Fast AGI shakes him, because being early with the tools **no longer helps**.
He'd turn toward **home retrofitting**, fixing the damp flats he sees in claims.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, where curiosity doesn't save him and he has no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Guaranteed **redeployment** instead of 'role at risk' letters.
